source: Zhang, Gray, Savelka, Ashley (2025) Measuring Faithfulness and Abstention: automated pipeline for LLM-generated 3-ply case-based legal arguments (faithfulness)
finding: Eight LLMs wrote HYPO/CATO-style 3-ply arguments from a current case plus two precedents given as factor lists (26 CATO trade-secret factors). They rarely invented factors.
numbers: 30 triples per test, complexity 12. Hallucination accuracy on Test 1 (arguable): 91.38% (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-70B) to 99.64% (GPT-4o). Test 2 (swapped precedent roles): 90.26% to 98.15%. Evaluator: GPT-4.1.
limits: Synthetic factor triples, not real opinions. Factors were given, not extracted. The evaluator is itself an LLM (spot checks only).
agent_relevance: Mapping to an analogue is not where models fail on faithfulness. Still check by code that every cited feature exists in the inputs (set difference).

source: Zhang, Gray, Savelka, Ashley (2025) Measuring Faithfulness and Abstention: automated pipeline for LLM-generated 3-ply case-based legal arguments (factor utilization)
finding: Recall of the available shared factors was far lower than faithfulness. Arguments were true but incomplete.
numbers: Factor utilization recall, Test 1 / Test 2 (%): GPT-4o 85.22/76.61; Llama-3-70B 77.51/74.62; DeepSeek-R1-Distill 72.61/69.58; Llama-4-Scout 69.47/63.77; Llama-3-8B 64.63/61.42; Llama-4-Maverick 53.95/51.40; GPT-4o-mini 42.47/49.55.
limits: Same synthetic setup. Recall depends on how many factors the evaluator can extract from prose.
agent_relevance: When mapping an analogue, enumerate all shared and unshared features in code and make the model address each, instead of trusting a free-form comparison.

source: Zhang, Gray, Savelka, Ashley (2025) Measuring Faithfulness and Abstention: automated pipeline for LLM-generated 3-ply case-based legal arguments (abstention test)
finding: When the precedents shared no factors with the current case and the prompt said to stop, most models wrote an argument anyway. Strong generators were not the best at abstaining.
numbers: Test 3 abstention ratio: GPT-4o 86.67%; Qwen-QWQ-32B 56.67%; Llama-4-Maverick 50.00%; DeepSeek-R1-Distill 23.33%; Llama-3-70B 3.33%; Llama-3-8B, Llama-4-Scout, GPT-4o-mini 0.00%. N = 30 non-arguable triples.
quote: The inability to reliably recognize task impossibility and adhere to negative constraints is a major concern
limits: One prompt wording for the negative constraint; behaviour may differ with other wording. Small N per cell.
agent_relevance: A nearest case that shares nothing must be a stop signal. Code should compute overlap and refuse to call the analogue operator when overlap is zero (G1, G3).

source: Zhang, Grabmair, Gray, Ashley (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: LLM capabilities in hierarchical legal reasoning (task ladder)
finding: Distinguishing a precedent from a current case was split into 3 tasks on CATO-style factors with a factor hierarchy. Accuracy fell sharply as steps were chained.
numbers: 253 test instances per task, exact set match, 6 models. Task 1 (find distinctions): 100% for all. Task 2 (hierarchical argumentative support): 64.82% (gemini-2.5-flash) to 92.09% (gpt-5). Task 3 (identify significant distinctions): 11.46% (gemini-flash) to 33.99% (qwen3-235b-thinking); most under 25%.
limits: Synthetic factor sets with ground truth from fixed rules. Real opinions are messier. Exact-match scoring is strict.
agent_relevance: Mapping an analogue works when it is one step. Chained judgement (which differences matter) is where reasoners fail. Split it into code-checked steps.

source: Zhang, Grabmair, Gray, Ashley (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: LLM capabilities in hierarchical legal reasoning (thinking effort)
finding: More thinking tokens went to wrong answers than right ones. Thinking mode helped a lot on the hierarchical task.
numbers: qwen3-thinking 78.66% vs non-thinking 30.04% on Task 2 (2.6x); on Task 3 non-thinking 0.00% vs thinking 33.99%. gpt-5 used 3,189 tokens for 92.09% on Task 2; qwen3-thinking used 9,596 tokens for 78.66%. gpt-5 wrong Task 2 answers averaged 4,456 tokens vs 3,081 for correct (+45%). Mean thinking tokens grew from 487 (Task 1) to 7,025 (Task 3).
quote: thinking longer does not always mean thinking smarter
limits: Six models, one benchmark. Token use is a correlate, not a cause.
agent_relevance: Token spend is a weak difficulty signal. Long reasoning is not a quality signal; do not reward length (G5).

source: Gray, Savelka, Oliver, Ashley (2024) Using LLMs to Discover Legal Factors
finding: LLMs proposed factors from raw opinions on reasonable suspicion in drug-interdiction stops; a human refined them; LLMs then annotated 174 cases and a classifier predicted outcomes. Fully automatic factor sets were the weakest.
numbers: 174 cases (71% suspicion found, 29% not). Metric MCC (ElasticNet / RandomForest). Gold expert annotation, canonical DIAS factors: 0.56 / 0.66. LLM annotating with canonical factors: llama 0.52 / 0.61, gpt-4o 0.32 / 0.41. LLM with human-refined factors: llama 0.56 / 0.46, gpt-4o 0.30 / 0.31. LLM with LLM-refined factors: 0.24 to 0.36 (ElasticNet) and 0.08 to 0.20 (RF). Span finding on 103 cases: accuracy 0.96, precision 0.99, recall 0.97.
limits: One legal domain, 80-20 split of a small set, one human refiner.
agent_relevance: Case representation is the bottleneck: LLM-built features without human review lost most predictive value. Keep a stable, reviewed feature list in memory instead of rebuilding it each run.

source: Zhang & Ashley (2026) Where Do Legal Factors Live in LLMs?
finding: All 26 CATO trade-secret factors are linearly decodable from the activations of three small open models, and a few sparse-autoencoder features carry most of it.
numbers: Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, Gemma-2 2B. Best-layer single-feature test AUC 0.86 to 1.00. Mean AUC at middle layer: 5 random features 0.551 / 0.534 / 0.578; 1 selected feature 0.944 / 0.954 / 0.950; 5 selected features 0.986 / 0.988 / 0.986. Human audit of 220 passages.
limits: Information present in activations is not information used in reasoning. Synthetic passages, small models, labels adjudicated by LLMs.
agent_relevance: The models probably hold the factor concepts, so failures in the 2025 and 2026 task studies are about composing and abstaining, not recognising features.

source: Guha et al. (2023) LegalBench
finding: A 162-task benchmark across six reasoning types. Applying a rule to facts is easier than recalling the rule.
numbers: Category means (issue, rule-recall, rule-conclusion, interpretation, rhetorical): GPT-4 82.9, 59.2, 89.9, 75.2, 79.4; GPT-3.5 60.9, 46.3, 78.0, 72.6, 66.7; Claude-1 58.1, 57.7, 79.5, 67.4, 68.9. Hand-graded rule-application (correctness / analysis): GPT-4 82.2 / 79.7; GPT-3.5 58.5 / 44.2; Claude-1 61.4 / 59.0.
limits: 2023 models. Few tasks require reasoning from precedent, so this is only indirect evidence for case-based reasoning.
agent_relevance: Recall of exact legal sources is the weak point, so supply the analogues in context instead of asking the model to remember them.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-Based Reasoning for Retrieval Augmented Generation in LLMs for Legal Question Answering
finding: Putting retrieved cases into the prompt beat no retrieval, but the gain was small. Full case text beat the support text alone in most variants.
numbers: Australian Open Legal QA, 2,124 question-answer pairs. Cosine similarity of generated answer to reference: No-RAG 0.8967; hybrid AnglEBERT k=1 support only 0.9121; best was hybrid AnglEBERT k=3 with full cases, +1.94% over No-RAG, significant at 95% (one-tailed t-test) against No-RAG and hybrid LegalBERT k=3, and at 90% against hybrid BERT k=1.
limits: Question-answer pairs were LLM-generated; metric is embedding cosine, not correctness. The No-RAG baseline was already high because of parametric memory. Small effect.
agent_relevance: Retrieved cases help only a little where the base model already knows the law. Test with a correctness metric on tasks the model has not memorised.

source: Tang et al. (2025) ReaKase-8B: Legal Case Retrieval via Knowledge and Reasoning Representations with LLMs
finding: Embedding a case with its extracted facts, issues, relation triplets and reasoning raised precedent retrieval over lexical and neural baselines on COLIEE.
numbers: COLIEE 2022 / 2023, mean of 5 runs, micro-F1: BM25 19.4 / 21.4; SAILER 14.0 / 16.6; PromptCase 18.5 / 20.8; Qwen3-8B 23.5 / 23.9; ReaKase-8B 27.0 / 28.7. MRR@5 ReaKase 52.7 / 48.1 vs BM25 23.6 / 23.1. Ablation NDCG@5 (2022): neither component 53.8, entities only 51.4, reasoning only 54.5, both 55.6. LEGAL-BERT 4.85 and MonoT5 0.60 micro-F1 (2022).
limits: Absolute F1 is still under 30, so most relevant cases are missed. Entities alone did not help in 2022 (51.4 vs 53.8).
agent_relevance: Retrieval by the reasoning behind a case beats surface similarity, but even the best system is weak. Store the reason for a decision, not only the outcome.

source: Sha et al. (2026) A Study of Prior Case Retrieval Using Lexical, Semantic, and Rhetorical Role Information in Indian Legal Documents
finding: A reported failure of validation: rankers with excellent internal scores did badly on the official test. A lexical baseline stayed strong.
numbers: Internal MRR up to 0.9711 but official MRR as low as 0.1414. Final four-stage pipeline: micro-F1 0.2549, MRR 0.6081, nDCG@10 0.4187. BM25 micro-F1@10 about 0.19 to 0.21. Test set: 237 queries, 1,727 candidate judgements.
limits: One shared task. Leakage explanation is the authors' own reading.
agent_relevance: Self-evaluation on data close to the fitting data is inflated. This supports G3: check against something the answer was not fitted to.

source: Fan et al. (2025) Legal Rule Induction: Towards Generalizable Principle Discovery from Analogous Judicial Precedents
finding: Asked to induce a general rule from 5 to 10 similar Chinese court cases, frontier LLMs over-generalised and hallucinated. LoRA fine-tuning of small models on 5,121 silver case sets closed much of the gap.
numbers: LRI-GOLD: 216 sets (108 criminal, 108 civil), three annotators. Direct micro-F1: GPT-4o 46.92, Gemini-2.5-Flash 55.50, Llama-4-Scout 60.51, Claude-3.7-Sonnet 66.67. Implicit-rule recall only about 25 to 48% for most direct models. Small models micro-F1 before / after LoRA: Llama-3.2-3B 19.21 / 70.96; Ministral-8B 52.53 / 73.18. Training set: 38,088 cases, 29,650 rules.
limits: Chinese law. Silver rules were produced by DeepSeek-R1 (audit of 100 sets found most correct). Fine-tuned models may learn corpus style.
agent_relevance: Inducing a rule from several analogues is harder than reading one. Generalise only from several cases and test the new rule on held-out cases.

source: Suttle & Lillis (2026) Assessing and Explaining the Persuadability of LLMs as Legal Decision Tools
finding: Judge LLMs deciding hard legal questions were swayed by advocate quality, and positional bias contributed.
numbers: Advocate quality had an average effect of 8% to 21%; stronger Advocate models won 58% to 71% of the time; strongest vs weakest 63% to over 90% depending on the judge. All persuasive effects significant.
limits: Hard questions chosen by the authors; effects vary strongly by judge model. Not a precedent-only study.
agent_relevance: If the agent weighs analogues for and against a position, rhetorical strength sways the verdict. Randomise order and hide the source of each argument (G5).

source: Suttle & Lillis (2026) Persuadability (order effects)
finding: Reversing party order had effects beyond a consistent positional bias, and the three-party set-up (two advocates, one judge) gave different apparent persuadability than a two-party set-up.
numbers: Win rates by advocate pairing with 95% CIs; the GPT-4o vs GPT-5.1 pairing gave the largest pairwise persuadability.
limits: Detailed table values were not extracted this session.
agent_relevance: Control argument order whenever the agent compares an analogue for and against.

source: Molfetta et al. (2026) Sycophants in the Courtroom: Are LLMs Fragile to Juridical Authority and Evolving Legal Standards?
finding: LLMs struggle to judge when retrieved legal citations are applicable, valid and non-contradictory, and are overconfident. Verified sources help in medicine but not reliably in law.
numbers: Abstract-level claim only; figure values were not verified this session.
limits: Only the abstract and a figure were read; headline numbers need a full read.
agent_relevance: A nearest case that is overruled or from the wrong jurisdiction looks like a good one. Keep a validity field in memory.

source: Liu, Lorini, Rotolo, Sartor (2022) Bridging Case-based Reasoning in Law and Reasoning about Classifiers
finding: Horty's factor-based theory of precedent is recast as a classifier logic: a case base maps feature sets to outcomes, and reasons and preferences between reasons become explanations of the classifier.
numbers: Formal results only; no empirical numbers.
limits: Theoretical. Does not test human or model behaviour.
agent_relevance: A case base is a classifier with constraints; memory can be implemented as a consistency check on the agent's own earlier decisions.

source: Prakken (2020) A Formal Analysis of some Factor- and Precedent-based Accounts of Precedential Constraint
finding: Formal comparison of factor and dimension models of precedential constraint, including Horty's and Rigoni's. Simple syntactic criteria say when a new case's decision is forced by a precedent.
numbers: Formal results only.
limits: Prakken says Rigoni's and (less) Horty's dimension-based reason models are limited in practice because they need information that may be hard to obtain.
agent_relevance: Gives a testable rule for when a precedent forces an answer: a check the code can run, with no model opinion.

source: Prakken & van Woerkom (2025) Defending the Hierarchical Result Models of Precedential Constraint
finding: A live dispute: Bench-Capon argued hierarchical result models give wrong outcomes when intermediate factors are established with different strengths; the authors reply that he treats intermediate factors as dimensions.
numbers: No numbers; argument by counterexample.
limits: Unresolved in the text read. No empirical test of which model fits courts.
agent_relevance: The right formalisation of precedent is contested, so treat any single similarity rule as a hypothesis, not as law.

source: Bench-Capon (1999) Some Observations on Modelling Case Based Reasoning with Formal Argument Models (ICAIL-99)
finding: Rule-based and case-based legal reasoning are not opposed: with independent boolean factors, precedents act as priority rules between sets of factors, forming a partial order. Quantified dimensions (HYPO) and factor hierarchies (CATO) break the simple picture.
numbers: Worked examples; no experiments.
quote: Prakken and Sartor's work gives a valuable insight into how these two approaches can be seen as not in conflict
limits: Needs boolean, independent factors.
agent_relevance: Legal CBR is rules plus priorities learned from cases, so memory can be a rule set with priority edges.

source: Bench-Capon (2012) Representing Popov v Hayashi with Dimensions and Factors
finding: One case represented with factors, with dimensions, with theory construction and with argumentation schemes. Different representations lead to different arguments. Theory-construction work was tested in programme experiments (Chorley and Bench-Capon 2005, cited, not read).
numbers: Four wild-animal precedents plus Popov. No statistics.
limits: Single worked case.
agent_relevance: The choice of representation changes the answer. When two representations of one case disagree, treat it as an impasse signal.

source: Bench-Capon (2004) review of Roth (2003) Case-based Reasoning in the Law: A Formal Theory of Reasoning by Case Comparison
finding: Review of a thesis that reconstructs HYPO, CABARET, CATO, IBP and GREBE in one formal model built on Reason Based Logic and a dialectical tree of factors.
numbers: 181-page thesis; no experiment reported in the review.
limits: Review only.
agent_relevance: Shows the lineage HYPO, CATO, IBP, where prediction was added after argument.

source: Bruninghaus & Ashley (2003) Predicting outcomes of case-based legal arguments (IBP)
finding: Recalled, not opened. The Issue-Based Prediction system predicts outcomes from factors plus issue structure and was reported to beat flat baselines on trade-secret cases.
numbers: Recalled: about 91% accuracy on 186 cases. Verify before use.
limits: Not opened this session; numbers from memory.
agent_relevance: Evidence that issue structure beats flat similarity, to verify.

source: Aleven (2003) Using background knowledge in case-based legal reasoning (CATO evaluation)
finding: Recalled, not opened. Law students taught case comparison with the CATO tool were reported to do about as well as those taught by a human instructor.
numbers: No figures recalled with confidence.
limits: Not opened this session; student samples small. Verify.
agent_relevance: Training for case comparison can be scaffolded by a factor tool.
